preregistration.expectation: Build one shared harness that runs the frozen, byte-identical job-recovery fixture (blueprints/convergence-practice/job-recovery/fixture.py with the unchanged planner and 12-test oracle) on Dagu 2.16.6, Prefect 3.8.6 (fresh uv venv, new prefix, local `prefect server start` on loopback) and a Temporal dev server (temporal CLI 1.9.1 release archive checksum-verified, temporalio 1.33.0 in a fresh venv). Cases: stop (engine-native stop/cancel while finalize waits), retry (engine-native retry of the same run), checkpoint reuse (claim count 1, checkpoint sha unchanged, 12 tests before/after) and SIGKILL (SIGKILL the executor process group mid-finalize, then an engine-native recovery attempt bounded at 150 s). Record the same oracle fields as run_parity.py. Expected: Dagu passes stop/retry/reuse and its SIGKILL recovery is refused without a scheduler (as #87 saw); Temporal passes all four (reset for retry; activity heartbeat timeout for SIGKILL); Prefect passes stop/retry/reuse via flow.serve + `prefect flow-run cancel/retry`, and its SIGKILL case leaves the run Running (uncertain).
preregistration.criteria: Settled iff the harness exists in the repository and executed all four cases on both Prefect and Temporal (pass or fail are both results), each installed at a pinned version in a new prefix, with the run_parity.py oracle fields recorded per engine. Restate is outside the next_check and is named as not covered. If either challenger cannot run a case, outcome is advanced with the missing case named.

outcome_detail: A shared harness now exists in the repository (blueprints/gap-wave2-20260923/foundation__scheduling-supervision/challenger/) and ran the frozen job-recovery fixture's stop, retry, checkpoint-reuse and SIGKILL cases on Prefect 3.8.6 and a Temporal dev server (and on Dagu 2.16.6), each installed at a pinned version in a new prefix, recording the run_parity.py oracle fields (before/after status, same run id, checkpoint execution count and sha256, 12/12 tests, owned processes remaining, finalizer retirement, model_calls 0). A Temporal or Prefect comparison therefore no longer needs new project work before it can run. The gap text also names Restate, and Restate was not ported: a Restate comparison still needs new project work (a Restate adapter class in compare.py, a pinned restate-server binary and Python SDK in a new prefix, and its native cancel/retry/recovery verbs). Outcome advanced (fix round 1; originally recorded as settled because the preregistered criteria excluded Restate, which did not close every clause of the gap text). SIGKILL results are reported under the preregistered protocol and 150 s bound (Dagu false, Prefect false, Temporal true) and, labelled as a post-hoc deviation, under a Dagu scheduler variant with a 270 s window (Dagu true at about 182 s).
limits: One run per engine per scenario on one WSL2 host for Prefect and Temporal (original run, 270 s window); Dagu SIGKILL ran three times (original scheduler variant, fix-round F1 preregistered protocol, fix-round F2 scheduler variant). Prefect's documented zombie-flow detection (flow-run heartbeats plus an automation) was not configured, while Temporal was given its recovery mechanism (a 5 s activity heartbeat timeout) and Dagu its scheduler in the variant; with zombie-flow detection configured, Prefect's SIGKILL result could differ.

Protocol deviation: the original run's Dagu scheduler (present from the first Dagu debug iteration) and its 270 s window (chosen after cmp-debug-p3 was seen) were not preregistered; they are labelled as a late deviation, and the preregistered protocol was executed in fix round 1 (F1). The fix-round preregistration itself was written after the review and is labelled as such.

The Temporal port needs adapter code to stop a subprocess on cancellation (heartbeat-driven); Dagu and Prefect stop step processes natively. Temporal's retry is a history reset that creates a new run id under the same workflow id; the oracle's same_native_run_id is recorded by workflow id and the run ids are listed.

The original run's Dagu scheduler (SIGKILL arm) bound its /health server on :8090 on all interfaces for about 3 minutes (and for 30 s in debug iteration cmp-debug-p3, 23:03:05-23:03:35-04:00) (Dagu binds ':<port>'; internal/service/healthcheck/server.go), departing from the loopback-only rule. Fix round 1 set scheduler.port 0 and verified no listener (F2).

Four development iterations preceded the original reported run (results retained in raw/4-6-debug-iterations/); they fixed harness defects (zombie processes counted as alive; a Prefect runner helper counted as run-scoped), and, not disclosed at the time, the SIGKILL window was raised from 30 s to 270 s after the Dagu result of cmp-debug-p3 was seen (see the deviation result).

No model calls, no broker, no paid API. All servers used loopback ports (except the disclosed original Dagu scheduler bind; the separate unit-level incident bind is described in the next limit) and temp data under the cache; every started process was stopped (leftover lists in each result.json name only the driver and, in fix round 1, the unit's own wait loop).

Unit-level isolation (fix round 2 cross-reference): this receipt's isolation statements cover this gap's own runs only. During fix round 1, between the fix-round preregistration and the F1/F2/F3 reruns, an unquoted heredoc started an unintended `dagu scheduler` (PATH dagu, default config) that wrote state into the default Dagu home $HOME/.local/share/dagu/data and bound :8090 on all interfaces for about 2 min 15 s, and an unintended `codex exec` that was killed while waiting for stdin. Fix round 2 verified that the running host `dagu server` (pid 366, the dagu-equities service) uses DAGU_HOME=$HOME/.local/share/codex-ecosystem/dagu-equities, a different store. See incidents/2026-09-22-fix-round-heredoc-substitution.json.

Resource rule (fix round 3): the Prefect 3.8.6 tree (104 distributions, 207.9 MB installed including run-time __pycache__) was installed with a plain `uv pip install`, not through ecosystem-bounded-run. The installed size is above the 200 MB figure and the tree is large, so the wave's heavy-build rule applied and was not followed; the compressed download was probably smaller, but its size was not recorded. The temporalio tree is 5 distributions, 56.6 MB installed. Both resolved sets are now recorded (resolved_dependency_sets; raw/fix3/venv-*-freeze.txt), so the environments can be rebuilt with `uv pip install -r` of the freeze files.

Only one gated model call was made in the whole unit (fix-round F3, gap 2); it waited 0 s with 0 other processes counted by the old matcher, so the timeout path was not reached. resolved_dependency_sets.set_is_the_executed_set: The raw files print three unlabelled epoch lines under a heading that says 'dist-info birth min/max and mtime max (epoch + iso)'; no ISO value is printed. Prefect: 1790131910 on all three lines (2026-09-22T22:51:50-04:00). temporalio: 1790131911 on all three lines (22:51:51-04:00). pyvenv.cfg was born 22:51:49.6 (prefect) and 22:51:50.6 (temporalio). So the dist-info directories were born 22:51:50-22:51:51, the install. The frozen set is the executed set because a reinstall or added package would create a dist-info directory with a later birth, and the newest dist-info birth equals the install time; the comparison started at 23:03 and the first debug iteration at 22:55:13. The separate check headed 'any file in venv modified after newest dist-info birth + 600 s' printed nothing, but its exit status, file filter (whether .pyc was excluded) and a detection control were not recorded, and its 600 s grace window (to about 23:01:51) covers the first debug iterations (cmp-debug-t-1790132113 = 22:55:13). It therefore does not show that no file changed after the install; it adds nothing beyond the dist-info birth argument.
resolved_dependency_sets.download_bytes: Not recorded at install time and not recoverable: the uv cache stores unpacked archives. The installed sizes include __pycache__ written when the engines ran, so they are an upper-bound proxy, not a measured download.
